reasons: The lake identity record verifies the case as State of Tennessee v. James Robert Christensen, Jr., court Tenn., decided 2017-04-07, year 2017, docket W2014-00931-SC-R11-CD.
The lake citation fields disclose official/display citation 2017 Tenn. LEXIS 195, parallel citation 517 S.W.3d 60, and vendor-neutral citation 2017 WL 1291657.

The opinion frames the issue as whether posted No Trespassing signs near an unobstructed driveway revoked or limited the invitation/license for police to conduct a warrantless knock-and-talk encounter.

The conclusion holds that officers did not violate constitutional search-and-seizure protections when they drove down the unobstructed driveway past No Trespassing signs and approached the residence to conduct a knock-and-talk consensual encounter.
residual_risks: The disclosed files do not define the corpus taxonomy for the role label Key, but the opinion text verifies that knock-and-talk is central to the case.

defect.evidence_quote: We emphasize that this approach recognizes the possibility that a sign, under the right circumstances, could be sufficient to revoke the implied license. Accordingly, we also emphasize that we are not adopting a per se rule in this case.
defect.locator_note: text/State v. Christensen__1fdbe9.txt, footnote 9; see also paragraph b92-6 for 'may be sufficient' language.
defect.problem: The holding overstates the physical-barrier rule. The opinion supports that No Trespassing signs near an unobstructed driveway were insufficient by themselves, but it does not hold that only barriers like a fence and closed gate will revoke the implied license. It says such barriers may be sufficient in some instances and expressly rejects a per se rule.
defect.proposed_fix: State that No Trespassing signs posted near an unobstructed driveway do not, by themselves and under the totality of the circumstances here, revoke the Jardines implied license for a constitutionally bounded knock-and-talk; physical barriers such as a fence and closed gate may be sufficient in some instances, but Christensen did not adopt an exclusive physical-barrier rule.

reasons: The first clause is supported: the opinion holds that, under the totality of the circumstances, the defendant's No Trespassing signs near his unobstructed driveway were not sufficient to revoke the Jardines implied license.
The second clause is overbroad: paragraph b92-6 says a fence and a closed gate that physically block access, in some instances, may be sufficient, not that only such barriers will suffice.
Footnote 9 expressly says a sign could be sufficient under the right circumstances and that the court was not adopting a per se rule.
residual_risks: The lake record contains no pinpoints, so support review relies on the cached opinion text.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Replace 'only barriers like a fence and closed gate that physically block access will do so' with 'clearer objective circumstances, such as a fence and closed gate physically blocking access, may be sufficient in some instances.'
